title: Unconditional Security of Discrete-Modulated CV-QKD from Infinite-Dimensional MEAT
summary: Discrete-Modulated (DM) Continuous-Variable (CV) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an experimentally attractive approach to quantum cryptography, offering high key rates over metropolitan-scale distances while relying on state-of-the-art telecom infrastructure. However, a fundamental gap has remained between this experimental promise and rigorous security: for more than two decades, DM CV-QKD has lacked a complete composable finite-size security proof against coherent attacks. Existing works either restrict the adversary to collective attacks, impose additional finite-dimensional assumptions, apply only to specific modulation formats, or fail to recover the known asymptotic rates. Here, we resolve this longstanding problem by establishing the first complete composable finite-size security proof for DM CV-QKD protocols against coherent attacks, incorporating imperfect detectors and both fixed- and variable-length protocol variants. Our proof introduces two central results of broader interest: an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (iMEAT) and a rigorous dimension-reduction technique that makes the infinite-dimensional security bounds numerically tractable. The resulting key rates recover the known asymptotic rates and outperform established finite-size bounds based on collective attacks, while yielding positive key rates beyond $70$km for experimentally relevant block sizes and parameters. Thus, our work closes a longstanding gap and places an experimentally attractive class of CV-QKD protocols on a rigorous composable security footing and provides a pathway towards their practical deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the first complete composable finite-size security proof for discrete-modulated continuous-variable QKD against coherent attacks, using an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem and a dimension-reduction technique.
AI.motivation: DM CV-QKD is experimentally attractive with high key rates over metropolitan distances, but for over two decades it lacked a complete composable finite-size security proof against coherent attacks. Prior works were limited to collective attacks, finite-dimensional assumptions, specific modulation formats, or failed to recover asymptotic rates.
AI.method: The authors develop an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (iMEAT) and a rigorous dimension-reduction technique to make infinite-dimensional security bounds numerically tractable. The proof incorporates imperfect detectors and covers both fixed- and variable-length protocol variants.
AI.result: The derived key rates recover the known asymptotic rates and outperform established finite-size bounds based on collective attacks. Positive key rates are obtained beyond 70 km for experimentally relevant block sizes and parameters.
AI.conclusion: The work closes a longstanding gap by placing an experimentally attractive class of CV-QKD protocols on a rigorous composable security footing and provides a pathway toward their practical deployment.

title: Direct Observation of Dipolar-Driven Anisotropic Quantum Projection Noise in a Solid-State Spin Ensemble
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond is a prominent quantum-sensing platform. Combining readout at the quantum projection noise limit with strong dipolar interactions promises substantial gains in sensitivity. However, experimentally accessing this regime has remained a longstanding challenge. In this work, we demonstrate quantum-projection-noise-resolved readout of a strongly-interacting, two-dimensional ensemble of NV centers. Our approach leverages repetitive readout via the NV's intrinsic $^{15}$N nuclear memory at a moderate magnetic field ($\sim 0.3$ T), improving the readout fidelities by nearly an order of magnitude. This enables us to directly resolve the quantum projection noise of a coherent spin state and to watch the ensemble's intrinsic dipolar interactions shear this noise into an anisotropic profile. Our results open the door to direct measurements of spin squeezing and entanglement-enhanced sensing in the solid state.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates quantum-projection-noise-resolved readout of a strongly-interacting 2D NV ensemble via repetitive readout using the intrinsic 15N nuclear memory, resolving coherent-state projection noise and watching dipolar interactions shear it into an anisotropic profile.
AI.motivation: Combining quantum-projection-noise-limited readout with strong dipolar interactions promises major sensitivity gains, but reaching this regime experimentally has been a longstanding challenge.
AI.method: Repetitive readout protocol exploiting the NV's intrinsic 15N nuclear memory at a moderate magnetic field (~0.3 T), enhancing readout fidelity by nearly an order of magnitude, applied to a strongly-interacting 2D NV ensemble.
AI.result: Readout fidelities improved by nearly an order of magnitude; direct resolution of the quantum projection noise of a coherent spin state; observation of intrinsic dipolar interactions shearing this noise into an anisotropic profile.
AI.conclusion: The results enable direct measurements of spin squeezing and entanglement-enhanced sensing in the solid state.

title: Large-scale quantum simulations of dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chains
summary: A quantum many-body system coupled to an environment relaxes to a nonequilibrium steady state that can sustain order with no equilibrium counterpart. Computing such steady states is harder than closed-system dynamics as the density matrix problem squares the Hilbert-space dimension, and no free energy selects the steady state. The dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain is a benchmark example for nonequilibrium steady state physics; various methods have each calculated its phase diagram but do not agree, and a controlled determination at large system size has remained out of reach. Here we simulate the Lindblad dynamics of chains of up to 50 sites on the superconducting processor ibm_kingston -- 100 simultaneously active qubits at up to 1700 entangling-gate depths -- realizing the dissipation via Stinespring dilation. The system's dissipative evolution is a self-correcting mechanism that effectively erases errors, so hardware noise enters only as a weak competing dissipator. We measure static structure factors and resolve ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-density-wave, and paramagnetic steady states, mapping the phase diagram with 117 quantum hardware data points across the $J_x$--$J_y$ plane. We uncover a rich non-equilibrium phase diagram of ordered phases with only remnants of the mean-field order, and where sharp transitions give way to the crossovers expected in one dimension. We also find the existence of an incipient (Trotter-induced) spin density wave phase, highlighting the potential of controlled Trotterization as a tool to engineer various magnetic phases in dissipative spin systems. Our quantum simulations largely settle the lingering uncertainty regarding the correct phase diagram of this benchmark system. Moreover, they show that quantum computers are now a feasible tool for addressing scientific questions involving dissipative quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The authors simulate the Lindblad dynamics of dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chains up to 50 sites on the superconducting processor ibm_kingston, realizing dissipation via Stinespring dilation, and map the nonequilibrium steady-state phase diagram in the Jx–Jy plane with 117 hardware data points, resolving ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-density-wave, and paramagnetic phases.
AI.motivation: Nonequilibrium steady states of open quantum many-body systems can sustain order with no equilibrium counterpart, but computing them is intractable in general: the density-matrix formulation squares the Hilbert-space dimension and no free energy selects the steady state. The dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain is a benchmark whose phase diagram remains contested, with existing methods disagreeing and no controlled large-size determination available.
AI.method: Quantum simulation of Lindblad dynamics on the superconducting processor ibm_kingston, with chains of up to 50 sites using 100 simultaneously active qubits and entangling-gate depths up to 1700. Dissipation is implemented through Stinespring dilation. The dissipative evolution acts as a self-correcting mechanism that effectively erases errors, so hardware noise enters only as a weak competing dissipator. Static structure factors are measured to characterize the steady states, and the phase diagram is mapped with 117 quantum hardware data points across the Jx–Jy plane.
AI.result: Ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-density-wave, and paramagnetic steady states are resolved. A rich nonequilibrium phase diagram is obtained, featuring ordered phases with only remnants of mean-field order, sharp transitions replaced by crossovers as expected in one dimension, and an incipient Trotter-induced spin-density-wave phase.
AI.conclusion: The quantum simulations largely settle the long-standing uncertainty regarding the correct phase diagram of the dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain, and demonstrate that quantum computers are now a feasible tool for addressing scientific questions about dissipative quantum systems. Controlled Trotterization is highlighted as a potential route to engineer magnetic phases in dissipative spin systems.

title: Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the GRASP2018 Package: Core Correlations
summary: The paper presents a further development of the method G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, L. Kitovienė, Second-Order of Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the {\sc Grasp}2018 Package: Core-Valence Correlations, {\em Lithuanian Journal of Physics}, 64, No. 1, 20-39 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.3952/physics.2024.64.1.3), based on a combination of the relativistic configuration interaction method and on the stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in an irreducible tensorial form. In this extension the perturbation theory accounts for both electron core-valence and core correlations when an atom or ion has any number of valence electrons meanwhile relativistic configuration interaction accounts for the rest of correlations. This allows a significant reduction of the space of the configuration state function for complex atoms and ions. We also demonstrate how this method works for energy structure calculation of Fe XV ion.

AI.tldr: Extended second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory combined with relativistic CI now accounts for both core-valence and core correlations for atoms/ions with arbitrary valence electron numbers, reducing configuration state function space; demonstrated on Fe XV energy structure.
AI.motivation: The prior method (core-valence correlations only) needed extension to include core correlations, and to be generally applicable to atoms/ions with any number of valence electrons, in order to handle complex systems while keeping the computational space tractable.
AI.method: Combination of the relativistic configuration interaction (RCI) method and stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in irreducible tensorial form. The perturbation theory treats both electron core-valence and core correlations; the RCI accounts for the remaining correlations. This permits significant reduction of the configuration state function (CSF) space.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated through energy structure calculation of the Fe XV ion, verifying its operation.
AI.conclusion: The extended approach enables accurate treatment of both core-valence and core correlations for complex atoms and ions with any number of valence electrons, significantly reducing the CSF space, as illustrated for Fe XV.

title: Adaptive detection of Rabi signals under composite hypotheses
summary: Motivated by searches for weak coherent drives, we formulate repeated quantum sensing with a fixed shot budget as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test. Taking Rabi sensing as a concrete example, we benchmark detection power, sensitivity, and Type-II error exponents in the resonant case with unknown signal amplitude and phase. We compare non-adaptive population and transverse readouts with a myopic Bayesian policy that selects each projective axis by maximizing the expected information gain in one step. The common decision statistic is a log Bayes factor, with a policy specific threshold calibrated under the null to enforce a common Type-I error. A weak signal expansion shows that population readout is phase independent but quadratic in amplitude, giving $n^{-1/4}$ sensitivity, whereas transverse readout is linear in amplitude and permits $n^{-1/2}$ sensitivity without adaptation, but is phase-dependent. In Monte Carlo pseudoexperiments, the adaptive policy exploits posterior information about the unknown direction to guide subsequent readouts; its sensitivity is consistent with $n^{-1/2}$ over the simulated large $n$ range and, at the largest simulated shot counts, outperforms the fixed transverse schedules. Its phase-averaged effective Type-II exponent also exceeds the non-adaptive references over the simulated range. These results demonstrate the finite budget value of exploiting nuisance parameter information under calibrated false positive control.

AI.tldr: This paper frames repeated quantum sensing under a fixed shot budget as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test, using Rabi sensing with unknown amplitude and phase. It benchmarks a myopic Bayesian adaptive readout policy against non-adaptive population and transverse readouts, showing the adaptive policy achieves n^{-1/2} sensitivity and better phase-averaged Type-II error exponents at large shot counts.
AI.motivation: Searches for weak coherent drives require efficient use of limited sensing resources, yet the problem of how to allocate a fixed shot budget across repeated measurements under unknown nuisance parameters (signal amplitude and phase) had not been properly framed as a statistical hypothesis-testing problem with calibrated false-positive control.
AI.method: The problem is cast as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test with a fixed shot budget, exampled by Rabi sensing in the resonant case with unknown amplitude and phase. Three readout strategies are compared: non-adaptive population readout, non-adaptive transverse readout, and a myopic Bayesian policy that picks each projective axis by maximizing one-step expected information gain. A log Bayes factor serves as the common decision statistic, with a policy-specific threshold calibrated under the null to fix Type-I error. A weak-signal expansion and Monte Carlo pseudoexperiments are used to evaluate detection power, sensitivity, and Type-II error exponents.
AI.result: The weak-signal expansion shows population readout is phase-independent but quadratic in amplitude (n^{-1/4} sensitivity), while transverse readout is linear in amplitude and allows n^{-1/2} sensitivity without adaptation but is phase-dependent. In simulations, the adaptive policy exploits posterior information on the unknown direction to guide later readouts, giving sensitivity consistent with n^{-1/2} across the large-n range and outperforming fixed transverse schedules at the largest shot counts; its phase-averaged effective Type-II exponent also exceeds the non-adaptive references.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting nuisance-parameter information through adaptive measurement design delivers tangible finite-budget gains in quantum sensing while maintaining calibrated false-positive control.

title: Orbital-angular-momentum partition in hydrogen photoionization by a monochromatic vortex beam
summary: Understanding how optical orbital angular momentum (OAM) is transferred to matter requires treating recoil and translational motion alongside the internal electronic dynamics. We develop a center-of-mass-resolved theory of one-photon ionization of hydrogen by a monochromatic Laguerre--Gaussian beam and show that the Bessel-vortex photoelectron predicted in fixed-target models is a preparation-dependent limit. For a sharply defined atomic center-of-mass momentum, the recoil records the photon-cone azimuth, and tracing over it generally destroys the coherence required for a pure electron vortex. In the small-transverse-retardation regime, the optical OAM is transferred predominantly to the center-of-mass motion and hence, in the laboratory frame, to the proton. Finite-retardation corrections redistribute angular momentum between center-of-mass and relative motion, while an additional correlation contribution to the electron and proton angular momenta can be tuned through the spatial uncertainty of the atomic center of mass. These results reveal atomic recoil as a key element of OAM transfer in photoionization.

AI.tldr: A center-of-mass-resolved theory shows that the Bessel-vortex photoelectron of photoionization is only a preparation-dependent limit; recoil and translational motion govern how optical OAM is distributed between center-of-mass and electronic dynamics.
AI.motivation: Fixed-target models predict a pure Bessel-vortex photoelectron in one-photon ionization by an OAM beam, but such models neglect recoil and translational motion. Understanding OAM transfer to matter requires treating these alongside internal electronic dynamics.
AI.method: Develops a center-of-mass-resolved theory of one-photon ionization of hydrogen by a monochromatic Laguerre-Gaussian beam, examining the role of atomic center-of-mass momentum, transverse retardation, and center-of-mass spatial uncertainty.
AI.result: For a sharply defined center-of-mass momentum, recoil records the photon-cone azimuth, and tracing over it generally destroys the coherence needed for a pure electron vortex. In the small-transverse-retardation regime, optical OAM transfers predominantly to center-of-mass motion (hence the proton in the lab frame). Finite-retardation corrections redistribute angular momentum between center-of-mass and relative motion, and an additional correlation contribution to electron and proton angular momenta is tunable via the spatial uncertainty of the atomic center of mass.
AI.conclusion: Atomic recoil is a key element of OAM transfer in photoionization; the Bessel-vortex photoelectron is not a universal outcome but a preparation-dependent limit.

title: Gauged AKSZ sigma models
summary: We propose a new class of sigma models that extend AKSZ sigma models, which we refer to as gauged AKSZ sigma models. These models are constructed using QP-manifolds. The compatibility between the AKSZ structure and gauging is characterized by geometric conditions on the target graded manifold. As an example, we explicitly analyze the gauging of higher Courant sigma models in higher dimensions. When fluxes and boundaries are introduced into gauged higher Courant sigma models, generalizations of momentum maps and Hamiltonian $G$-spaces arise as consistency conditions for the models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces gauged AKSZ sigma models, a new class of sigma models extending AKSZ models, constructed via QP-manifolds with geometric compatibility conditions. It analyzes gauging of higher Courant sigma models, showing that fluxes and boundaries lead to generalized momentum maps and Hamiltonian G-spaces as consistency conditions.
AI.motivation: AKSZ sigma models provide a powerful framework, but gauging them (coupling to gauge fields while preserving the AKSZ structure) lacks a systematic construction. The paper aims to develop such a gauging procedure and understand the geometric conditions required for consistency.
AI.method: The authors construct gauged AKSZ sigma models using QP-manifolds. Compatibility between the AKSZ structure and gauging is encoded in geometric conditions on the target graded manifold. They explicitly work out the gauging of higher Courant sigma models in higher dimensions, and examine the effects of introducing fluxes and boundaries.
AI.result: A new class of gauged AKSZ sigma models is defined with geometric consistency conditions on the target graded manifold. For gauged higher Courant sigma models, the introduction of fluxes and boundaries yields generalized momentum maps and Hamiltonian G-spaces as consistency conditions.
AI.conclusion: Gauged AKSZ sigma models form a natural and consistent extension of AKSZ models, with gauging controlled by geometric conditions on the target graded manifold. The framework recovers and generalizes momentum maps and Hamiltonian G-spaces in the context of higher Courant sigma models with fluxes and boundaries.

title: The Transient Counting Statistics of Autonomous Quantum Clocks
summary: At the heart of every atomic clock is a quantum coherent emitter, the laser, that could in principle be treated autonomously. While their frequency or phase stability is typically studied in the semiclassical regime of a large number of emitted quanta, recent works on autonomous quantum clocks suggest that the few-quanta regime can offer statistical information in the temporal domain. This provides complementary means to probe the fundamental limits to precise timekeeping in the quantum regime. Motivated by these works, we consider simple models for two- and three-level quantum emitters subject to an athermal fueling through dephasing, which generically results in coherences in the steady state. A large deviation principle with finite-time contributions is used to identify the transient counting statistics and their dependence on the initial conditions. We conclude by discussing the implications for precise timekeeping and quantum sensing using autonomous quantum emitters as clocks in their transient regime.

AI.tldr: This work studies simple two- and three-level quantum emitters driven by athermal dephasing, using a large-deviation principle with finite-time corrections to characterize transient counting statistics and assess implications for quantum clocks and sensing.
AI.motivation: Atomic clocks rely on quantum coherent emitters (lasers), usually analyzed semiclassically with many emitted quanta. Recent autonomous quantum clock studies suggest the few-quanta regime carries temporal statistical information, offering a complementary route to probe fundamental limits of quantum timekeeping. This motivates examining simple emitter models in that regime.
AI.method: The authors consider simple models of two- and three-level quantum emitters subject to athermal fueling via dephasing, which generically produces steady-state coherences. They apply a large deviation principle including finite-time contributions to identify the transient counting statistics and their dependence on initial conditions.
AI.result: Transient counting statistics are identified via a finite-time large-deviation treatment, and their dependence on initial conditions is characterized.
AI.conclusion: The findings are discussed in terms of implications for precise timekeeping and quantum sensing using autonomous quantum emitters as clocks operated in their transient regime.

title: Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the GRASP2018 Package: Core-Core Correlations
summary: Grasp package is based on the relativistic configuration interaction in which accurate calculations, accounting for valence, valence-valence, core-valence, core, and core-core electron correlations, often rely on massive CSF expansions. This paper presents further development of the method based on the second-order perturbation theory for finding the most important CSFs that have the greatest influence on the core-valence, core, and core-core correlations. This method is based on a combination of the relativistic configuration interaction method and the stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in an irreducible tensorial form [G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, L. Kitovienė, Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the Grasp2018 Package: Core-Valence Correlations, Lithuanian Journal of Physics, 64, No. 1, 20-39 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.3952/physics.2024.64.1.3) and G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, L. Kitovienė, Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the Grasp2018 Package: Core Correlations, Lithuanian Journal of Physics, 64, No. 2, 73-81 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.3952/physics.2024.64.2.1)]. In this extension, the perturbation theory accounts for electron core-valence, core, and core-core correlations where an atom or ion has any number of valence electrons for calculation of energy spectra and other properties. Meanwhile the rest of the correlations are accounted for in a traditional way. This allows a significant reduction of the space of the configuration state function for complex atoms and ions. We also demonstrate how this method works for calculations of the energy structure and E1 transition properties of Fe XV ion.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a second-order perturbation theory method within the GRASP package to efficiently account for core-valence, core, and core-core electron correlations in relativistic configuration interaction calculations, using the Fe XV ion to demonstrate energy structure and E1 transition property calculations.
AI.motivation: Accurate calculations accounting for valence, valence-valence, core-valence, core, and core-core electron correlations in the GRASP relativistic configuration interaction framework often rely on massive configuration state function (CSF) expansions, which are computationally prohibitive for complex atoms and ions.
AI.method: The method combines relativistic configuration interaction with stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in an irreducible tensorial form. The extension accounts for core-valence, core, and core-core correlations using perturbation theory to identify the most influential CSFs, applicable to atoms or ions with any number of valence electrons, while remaining correlations are treated traditionally.
AI.result: The method significantly reduces the CSF space for complex atoms and ions. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through calculations of the energy structure and E1 transition properties of the Fe XV ion.
AI.conclusion: The extended perturbation-theory-based approach enables efficient and accurate treatment of core-valence, core, and core-core correlations within GRASP, offering substantial reduction in CSF expansion size for complex atomic systems, as validated by Fe XV energy structure and E1 transition calculations.

title: Reflectionless edge states in Dirac models of topological insulators
summary: We study an effective model of topological insulators joined along a bent interface. The Hamiltonian is a Dirac operator $\mathcal{D} = D_1σ_1 + D_2σ_2 + κ(x) σ_3$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2,\mathbb{C}^2)$, where $κ(x)$ represents a domain wall with a corner: while initially straight, it undergoes a bend when passing from one side of $\mathbb{R}^2$ to the other. For most energies in a spectral window centered at $0$, we construct a reflectionless edge state of $\mathcal{D}$: a distorted plane wave with transmission coefficient of modulus $1$. This implies that $\mathcal{D}$ admits modes confined near $κ^{-1}(\{0\})$, that travel through the bend with no loss neither to the bulk nor to reflection. Our result explains experimental observations from the physics literature, as well as our own numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a reflectionless edge state of a Dirac-type domain-wall Hamiltonian for a bent interface, showing a distorted plane wave with unit-modulus transmission across the corner, i.e., lossless transport with no bulk or reflection loss.
AI.motivation: An effective model of topological insulators joined along a bent interface is studied, motivated by the observation that topological edge modes appear able to traverse a bend without scattering. The goal is to rigorously explain such robust, lossless transmission through a corner observed in physics experiments and the authors' numerical simulations.
AI.method: A Dirac operator D = D1σ1 + D2σ2 + κ(x)σ3 on L^2(R^2,C^2) is analyzed, where κ(x) is a domain wall that is initially straight but bends when crossing from one side of R^2 to the other. For most energies in a spectral window centered at 0, the authors construct a reflectionless edge state of D, realized as a distorted plane wave whose transmission coefficient has modulus 1.
AI.result: For most energies in a spectral window centered at 0, D admits a reflectionless edge state with transmission coefficient of modulus 1, demonstrating modes confined near κ^{-1}({0}) that travel through the bend without loss to the bulk or to reflection.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a rigorous explanation for experimental observations in the physics literature as well as the authors' own numerical simulations, establishing lossless, reflection-free edge-mode transport through a bent domain wall in the effective Dirac model.

title: Hyperbolic color codes with constant rate and polynomial distance
summary: Recent advances in quantum hardware relax the strict geometric-locality constraints traditionally imposed on quantum error-correcting codes, motivating interest in high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. At the same time, color codes provide a particularly rich setting for fault-tolerant quantum computation, underlying protocols such as single-shot error correction and self-correcting quantum computation. Hyperbolic color codes provide a class of high-rate qLDPC codes that also retain the structural features of color codes relevant to fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, previous constructions of hyperbolic color codes have achieved at most logarithmic code distance. In this work, we construct hyperbolic color codes with both constant rate and polynomial distance by building on arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds that support polynomial-distance hyperbolic toric codes. Our construction applies in arbitrary dimension \(D\geq 4\). In even dimensions, the resulting type-\(D/2\) color codes have constant encoding rate and polynomial distance, while in other cases the number of logical qubits and the code distance both exhibit polynomial scaling. We further derive explicit exponents for polynomial lower bounds as functions of the dimension and code type. These results establish a family of hyperbolic color codes simultaneously achieving constant rate and polynomial distance and providing a testbed to explore fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols that combine high-rate quantum codes with the structural advantages of color codes.

AI.tldr: This work constructs hyperbolic color codes with constant rate and polynomial distance in arbitrary dimension D≥4, using arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds, overcoming the previous logarithmic-distance limitation.
AI.motivation: Quantum hardware advances relax geometric-locality constraints, spurring interest in high-rate qLDPC codes. Hyperbolic color codes combine high rate with color-code structure useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation (e.g., single-shot error correction, self-correcting computation), but prior constructions achieved at most logarithmic code distance.
AI.method: Build on arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds that support polynomial-distance hyperbolic toric codes to construct hyperbolic color codes in arbitrary dimension D≥4; derive explicit polynomial lower-bound exponents as functions of dimension and code type.
AI.result: In even dimensions, the type-D/2 color codes achieve constant encoding rate and polynomial distance; in other cases, both the number of logical qubits and the code distance scale polynomially. Explicit exponents for the polynomial lower bounds are derived.
AI.conclusion: A family of hyperbolic color codes simultaneously achieving constant rate and polynomial distance is established, providing a testbed for fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols combining high-rate quantum codes with the structural advantages of color codes.

title: Second-Order Rayleigh-Schrödinger Perturbation Theory for the Grasp2018 Package: Valence-Valence Correlations
summary: The accurate description of electron correlations remains a major challenge in atomic calculations. In order to perform accurate calculations, it is necessary to consider the various types of electron correlations what often leads to extensive CSF expansions. This work presents further development of the method based on the second-order perturbation theory to identify the most significant CSFs that have the greatest influence on core-valence, core, core-core and valence-valence correlations. This method is based on a combination of the relativistic configuration interaction method and the stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in an irreducible tensorial form [G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, L. Kitovienė, Lithuanian Journal of Physics, 64, No. 1, 20-39 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.3952/physics.2024.64.1.3), G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, L. Kitovienė, Lithuanian Journal of Physics, 64, No. 2, 73-81 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.3952/physics.2024.64.2.1) and G. Gaigalas, P. Rynkun, L. Kitovienė, Lithuanian Journal of Physics, 64, No. 3, 139-161 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.3952/physics.2024.64.3.1)]. The method is extended to include additionally valence-valence electron correlations. It can be applied for an atom or ion with any number of valence electrons for calculation of energy spectra and other properties. Meanwhile, the correlations which can not be included according to perturbation theory are accounted for in a regular way. The use of the developed method allows a significant reduction of CSFs especially for complex atoms and ions. As an example of its application, the atomic calculations of the energy structure for Se~III ion are presented.

AI.tldr: This work extends a second-order perturbation-theory-based CI method to include valence-valence correlations, enabling accurate atomic calculations with drastically reduced configuration state function (CSF) expansions, demonstrated on the Se III ion energy structure.
AI.motivation: Accurate description of electron correlations is a major challenge in atomic calculations. Capturing core-valence, core, core-core, and valence-valence correlations typically requires extensive CSF expansions, which becomes computationally prohibitive for complex atoms and ions. There is a need for a method that identifies only the most significant CSFs while retaining accuracy.
AI.method: The method combines the relativistic configuration interaction (RCI) approach with stationary second-order Rayleigh-Schrödinger many-body perturbation theory in an irreducible tensorial form. Originally developed to treat core-valence, core, and core-core correlations, it is here extended to additionally include valence-valence electron correlations. CSFs are ranked by their perturbative significance; residual correlations not captured by perturbation theory are treated in a regular (standard) manner. It is applicable to atoms or ions with any number of valence electrons.
AI.result: The extended method yields a significant reduction of CSFs, particularly for complex atoms and ions, while maintaining accurate energy spectra and other properties. As a demonstration, atomic calculations of the energy structure for the Se III ion were performed.
AI.conclusion: Extending the second-order perturbation-theory-based CI method to valence-valence correlations provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for atomic structure calculations, offering substantial CSF reduction and applicability to systems with arbitrary valence electron numbers.

title: Operator-theoretic and analytic properties of a driven single-mode Kerr cavity in Bargmann space
summary: We study the stationary spectrum of a coherently driven single-mode Kerr cavity in Bargmann--Fock space. For positive Kerr coupling the Hamiltonian is self-adjoint, bounded below, and has compact resolvent. For nonzero drive, a minimal-solution continued fraction yields an exact scalar spectral condition, with all eigenvalues simple. A Liouville transformation identifies the eigenvalue equation with a degenerate double-confluent Heun problem and classifies its singularities. An Olver-type Volterra construction gives normalized sectorial solutions at infinity with explicit error bounds. In the strong-drive regime, the leading turning-point energy coefficient is proved, whereas the next coefficient remains conditional on a stated global-connection conjecture; independent Bogoliubov and complex-WKB calculations provide consistency checks. A formal weak-drive expansion is verified from the Bargmann recurrence, and its upper-edge tridiagonal series is summed in closed form. Exploratory WKB iteration portraits are included only as visual aids and do not establish the conjectural global connection.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the stationary spectrum of a coherently driven single-mode Kerr cavity in Bargmann–Fock space, deriving an exact scalar spectral condition via continued fractions and connecting the eigenvalue problem to a degenerate double-confluent Heun equation, with rigorous strong-drive and formal weak-drive results.
AI.motivation: Understanding the spectrum of coherently driven Kerr cavities is central to nonlinear quantum optics, yet a mathematically rigorous spectral characterization—especially in the strong- and weak-drive regimes—remains incomplete.
AI.method: Bargmann–Fock space representation of the driven Kerr Hamiltonian; minimal-solution continued fraction for an exact scalar spectral condition; Liouville transformation to a degenerate double-confluent Heun problem with singularity classification; Olver-type Volterra construction for normalized sectorial solutions at infinity with explicit error bounds; Bogoliubov and complex-WKB consistency checks; formal weak-drive expansion and closed-form summation of the upper-edge tridiagonal series.
AI.result: For positive Kerr coupling the Hamiltonian is self-adjoint, bounded below, and has compact resolvent; for nonzero drive all eigenvalues are simple. The leading strong-drive turning-point energy coefficient is proved, while the next coefficient is conditional on a stated global-connection conjecture. Independent Bogoliubov and complex-WKB calculations agree, and the weak-drive expansion is verified from the Bargmann recurrence.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous spectral framework for the driven Kerr cavity, establishing exact spectral conditions and a Heun-equation connection, with the strong-drive leading coefficient proved and the subleading coefficient reduced to a global-connection conjecture; exploratory WKB portraits serve only as visual aids.

title: Pulse-Level Compilation of Measurement-Free Recovery in Transmon Circuits
summary: Quantum error correction commonly relies on syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback. We numerically show that the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit can compile a local recovery rule into a fixed open-loop control cycle. In a four-bit repetition-code ring, the resulting input-independent control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-\(X\) noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation relative to uncorrected references. Its local, bounded-degree architecture provides a hardware-native framework for extending compiled recovery control to larger quantum networks.

AI.tldr: An interacting transmon circuit's conditional spectrum can compile a local recovery rule into a fixed open-loop control cycle, slowing logical coherence decay under Pauli-X noise beyond uncorrected references.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum error correction relies on syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback, which imposes substantial hardware and latency overhead. The authors seek a hardware-native alternative that avoids these steps.
AI.method: Numerically demonstrate that the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit compiles a local recovery rule into a fixed, input-independent open-loop control cycle. This is implemented in a four-bit repetition-code ring with a local, bounded-degree architecture.
AI.result: The compiled open-loop control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-X noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation, both relative to uncorrected references.
AI.conclusion: Compiled recovery control in a local, bounded-degree architecture offers a hardware-native framework for extending this approach to larger quantum networks.

title: Improved calculation of the hyperfine structure of muonic helium
summary: Using perturbation theory for the fine-structure constant $α$ and the electron-to-muon mass ratio, we calculated new contributions to the hyperfine structure of the ground state of the muon-electron helium atom. Compared to our previous results, we calculated new corrections in second-order perturbation theory. This calculation reduces the discrepancy between the theoretical value and the new experimental hyperfine structure measurement.

AI.tldr: New second-order perturbation theory corrections to the hyperfine structure of the ground state of muonic helium improve agreement with recent experimental measurements.
AI.motivation: A discrepancy exists between the theoretical hyperfine structure value of the muon-electron helium atom ground state and recent experimental measurements.
AI.method: Perturbation theory in the fine-structure constant α and the electron-to-muon mass ratio, including newly computed second-order corrections.
AI.result: New contributions to the ground-state hyperfine structure were obtained, reducing the theory-experiment discrepancy.
AI.conclusion: Second-order perturbation theory corrections significantly improve the agreement between theory and the new experimental hyperfine structure measurement.

title: Diassociative conformal algebras and their deformation cohomology
summary: In this paper, we introduce diassociative conformal algebras that unify both associative conformal algebras and diassociative algebras. We show that the category of diassociative conformal algebras is equivalent to the category of equivalence classes of formal distribution diassociative algebras. By employing its Maurer-Cartan characterization, we then define the cohomology of a diassociative conformal algebra and show that it carries a Gerstenhaber algebra structure. Our cohomology can be used to study deformations and extensions of the structure. Finally, we define averaging operators on associative conformal algebras and find their close relations with diassociative conformal algebras.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces diassociative conformal algebras unifying associative conformal algebras and diassociative algebras, proves a category equivalence with equivalence classes of formal distribution diassociative algebras, defines a cohomology with Gerstenhaber algebra structure via Maurer-Cartan characterization, and applies it to deformations and extensions, alongside studying averaging operators on associative conformal algebras.
AI.motivation: Diassociative algebras and associative conformal algebras are two established structures, but a unified framework connecting them was lacking. The paper aims to bridge this gap by constructing a common generalization that captures the features of both settings.
AI.method: The authors define diassociative conformal algebras and establish an equivalence between their category and the category of equivalence classes of formal distribution diassociative algebras. Using a Maurer-Cartan characterization, they construct a cohomology theory for these algebras and equip it with a Gerstenhaber algebra structure. They further define averaging operators on associative conformal algebras.
AI.result: The category of diassociative conformal algebras is shown equivalent to the category of equivalence classes of formal distribution diassociative algebras. The proposed cohomology carries a Gerstenhaber algebra structure and is effective for studying deformations and extensions. Averaging operators on associative conformal algebras exhibit close relations with diassociative conformal algebras.
AI.conclusion: Diassociative conformal algebras serve as a unifying framework that connects diassociative algebras and associative conformal algebras, supports a cohomology theory with Gerstenhaber structure applicable to deformations and extensions, and links naturally to averaging operators on associative conformal algebras.

title: Designs without disorder: unitary $k$-designs from a single-site bulk defect
summary: We show that an $O(1)$ local defect is sufficient to generate approximate unitary $k$-designs from an otherwise integrable quantum many-body system. Using a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol with temporal sampling, we demonstrate this mechanism in a fixed-magnetization sector of deterministic XXZ spin chains with a single integrability-breaking bulk defect. We derive an analytical selection rule for the Pauli kicks and show that symmetry-preserving strings with a specific domain-wall count, fixed by the couplings, govern design formation. An exhaustive search over all admissible Pauli strings identifies a broad family of kicks that produce designs in the chaotic regime, whereas no such kicks exist in the integrable limit, including for boundary defects. We further show that the design-forming mechanism remains effective for weak bulk defects as the system size increases.

AI.tldr: An O(1) local defect suffices to generate approximate unitary k-designs from an otherwise integrable XXZ spin chain via a two-Pauli-kick protocol with temporal sampling.
AI.motivation: Integrable quantum many-body systems fail to scramble or form designs; the paper asks how minimal a perturbation must be to induce design formation, and whether boundary versus bulk defects differ.
AI.method: Two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol with temporal sampling applied to a fixed-magnetization sector of deterministic XXZ chains containing a single integrability-breaking bulk defect; analytical derivation of a Pauli-kick selection rule; exhaustive search over all admissible Pauli strings.
AI.result: A selection rule is derived showing that symmetry-preserving strings with a domain-wall count fixed by the couplings govern design formation. A broad family of kicks produces designs in the chaotic regime, while none exist in the integrable limit, including for boundary defects. The mechanism persists for weak bulk defects as system size grows.
AI.conclusion: A single O(1) bulk defect is sufficient to convert an integrable system into a generator of approximate unitary k-designs, and the effect is robust with increasing system size for weak defects.

title: Angle-of-Arrival Determination of Radio-Frequency Fields Using Stark-Shifted Rydberg-EIT Spectra
summary: We demonstrate a method for determining the magnitude of the angle of arrival (AoA) of a linearly polarized radio-frequency (RF) field using the angle-dependent spectral amplitudes of AC Stark-shifted electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) resonances. An off-resonant RF field produces distinct Stark shifts of the $|m_J|$ sublevels, while their relative excitation strengths depend strongly on the relative orientation of the RF and optical polarizations. Under the controlled polarization geometry considered here, this dependence enables determination of the AoA magnitude without requiring RF phase measurements or spatially separated sensing locations. We experimentally demonstrate the method at RF frequencies of 1.27 GHz, 2 GHz, 3 GHz, and 4 GHz using a subwavelength cesium vapor cell. Within the $20^\circ-40^\circ$ region of highest angular sensitivity, the estimated repeatability-based $1σ$ AoA uncertainty ranges from approximately $0.6^\circ$ to $2^\circ$ across the investigated RF frequencies. A model combining Floquet-Shirley calculations of the RF-dressed Rydberg states with a coherent hyperfine-to-fine-structure optical excitation model qualitatively reproduces the experimental observations. These results establish a path toward compact, phase-independent AoA sensing using spatially localized Rydberg-atom spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: A phase-independent method determines the angle-of-arrival magnitude of a linearly polarized RF field from the angle-dependent spectral amplitudes of AC Stark-shifted EIT resonances in a subwavelength cesium vapor cell, achieving ~0.6°–2° uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Conventional angle-of-arrival (AoA) sensing typically requires RF phase measurements or multiple spatially separated sensors. The authors aim to eliminate these requirements by exploiting the polarization-orientation dependence of AC Stark-shifted EIT resonances, enabling compact single-cell sensing.
AI.method: An off-resonant linearly polarized RF field AC-Stark-shifts the |mJ| sublevels of Rydberg states, and their relative excitation strengths depend on the relative orientation of RF and optical polarizations. Measuring the angle-dependent spectral amplitudes of EIT resonances under a controlled polarization geometry yields the AoA magnitude, without RF phase measurements or spatially separated locations. Experiments use a subwavelength cesium vapor cell at 1.27, 2, 3, and 4 GHz. Floquet-Shirley RF-dressed Rydberg calculations are combined with a coherent hyperfine-to-fine-structure optical excitation model.
AI.result: Within the 20°–40° high-sensitivity region, the repeatability-based 1σ AoA uncertainty is approximately 0.6°–2° across the investigated RF frequencies. The combined Floquet-Shirley and coherent optical excitation model qualitatively reproduces the experimental observations.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a route to compact, phase-independent AoA sensing via spatially localized Rydberg-atom spectroscopy, using a single subwavelength vapor cell without phase or spatial-separation requirements.

title: Higher abelian gauge theory in BV formalism
summary: A BV structure is constructed on the space of zero modes of a quadratic elliptic higher abelian gauge theory. The associated BV integral is shown to be independent of the choice of zero-mode Lagrangian under mild hypotheses. The construction yields explicit zero-mode partition functions for several $p$-form abelian gauge theories.

AI.tldr: A BV structure is built on the zero-mode space of a quadratic elliptic higher abelian gauge theory; the associated BV integral is Lagrangian-choice independent under mild hypotheses, yielding explicit zero-mode partition functions for several p-form abelian gauge theories.
AI.motivation: Zero modes of quadratic elliptic higher abelian gauge theories require a consistent quantization framework, and the dependence of the resulting partition function on auxiliary choices (such as the zero-mode Lagrangian) needs to be controlled.
AI.method: Construct a Batalin–Vilkovisky (BV) structure on the space of zero modes, then analyze the associated BV integral and its invariance under changes of the zero-mode Lagrangian.
AI.result: The BV integral is shown to be independent of the choice of zero-mode Lagrangian under mild hypotheses, and explicit zero-mode partition functions are obtained for several p-form abelian gauge theories.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a well-defined, choice-independent BV quantization of zero modes and delivers computable zero-mode partition functions for a class of higher abelian gauge theories.

title: Investigating Interacting Fermionic Models with Locality-Preserving Qubit Encodings
summary: We investigate the utility of the locality-preserving Derby-Klassen (DK) fermion-to-qubit mapping [arXiv:2003.06939] for variational quantum simulation of two-dimensional $t$-$V$ and Fermi-Hubbard models. The DK mapping preserves the locality of fermionic interactions with an enlarged Hilbert space, thereby requiring additional constraints that define the physical sector. We incorporate these constraints directly into a Hamiltonian Variational Ansätz (HVA) through Clifford-gate state preparation and use the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) to show that the low-energy properties of the resulting qubit Hamiltonian are accurately reproduced. We further exploit particle-number conservation inherent in the ansätz to resolve distinct symmetry sectors and reliably access degenerate states. Consequently, we benchmark the DK-HVA against Jordan-Wigner-based variational circuits at nonzero chemical potential, where particle-hole symmetry and the associated half-filled sign-free condition are absent. Finally, we demonstrate the advantage of locality-preserving mappings in higher-dimensional fermionic systems, where the conventional Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation generates increasingly long Pauli strings and corresponding circuit overheads. We further extend the framework to the spinful Fermi-Hubbard model and identify a tradeoff between fermionic-mode placement and the locality of hopping and on-site interaction terms. These results establish a practical framework combining locality-preserving fermion-to-qubit mappings, constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation, and symmetry-preserving variational circuits, that trades auxiliary-qubit and stabilizer-preparation overhead for reduced operator nonlocality, providing a practical route toward resource-efficient quantum simulation of higher-dimensional interacting fermionic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks a locality-preserving Derby–Klassen (DK) fermion-to-qubit mapping combined with a constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation and a Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz (HVA) for VQE simulation of 2D t-V and Fermi-Hubbard models, showing accurate low-energy spectra, symmetry-sector resolution, and a locality advantage over Jordan-Wigner in higher dimensions.
AI.motivation: Simulating interacting fermionic systems in two dimensions is classically hard and promising for quantum advantage, but the standard Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation produces increasingly long Pauli strings as dimensionality grows, causing substantial circuit overhead. Locality-preserving mappings such as DK can mitigate nonlocality but require an enlarged Hilbert space with auxiliary constraints defining the physical sector, which must be handled at the circuit level.
AI.method: The authors use the locality-preserving Derby-Klassen fermion-to-qubit mapping and embed its physical-sector constraints directly into a Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz via Clifford-gate state preparation. They run VQE on the resulting qubit Hamiltonian for 2D t-V and spinful Fermi-Hubbard models, exploiting particle-number conservation in the ansatz to resolve distinct symmetry sectors and access degenerate states. They benchmark DK-HVA against JW-based variational circuits at nonzero chemical potential, and analyze fermionic-mode placement tradeoffs between hopping and on-site interaction locality.
AI.result: The DK-based ansatz accurately reproduces low-energy properties of the qubit Hamiltonian, reliably accesses degenerate states across symmetry sectors, and outperforms JW-based circuits at nonzero chemical potential where particle-hole symmetry and the half-filled sign-free condition are absent. Locality-preserving mappings show clear advantages in higher-dimensional fermionic systems, and an explicit tradeoff is identified between fermionic-mode placement and the locality of hopping versus on-site interaction terms.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a practical framework that combines locality-preserving fermion-to-qubit mappings, constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation, and symmetry-preserving variational circuits. It trades auxiliary-qubit and stabilizer-preparation overhead for reduced operator nonlocality, offering a resource-efficient route to quantum simulation of higher-dimensional interacting fermionic systems.

title: Optimal Linear-Rate Conversion of Unknown Mixed Qubit States via SWAP Tests
comment: 5 pages main body + appendices; 1 table and 1 figure; comments welcome!
summary: By consuming multiple copies of an unknown qubit state, one can modify its purity while preserving the direction of its Bloch vector. We determine the maximum linear rate at which qubit states of different purities can be interconverted, allowing a nonzero error, quantified, for instance, by the trace distance, provided that it vanishes in the limit of infinitely many copies. Interestingly, the optimal conversion rate is determined by the two eigenvalues of the complex right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information matrix associated with $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ rotations of the qubit state. When the output qubits have higher purity, corresponding to concentration, the optimal rate is given by the ratio of the maximum eigenvalues of the input and output RLD matrices. In contrast, when the output qubits have lower purity, corresponding to dilution, the optimal rate is given by the ratio of their minimum eigenvalues. Remarkably, both concentration and dilution can be implemented using SWAP tests as the only nontrivial two-qubit measurement primitive, together with ancillary qubits initially prepared in maximally mixed states, without requiring any additional two-qubit gates. Our work thus provides a novel operational interpretation of the full complex RLD Fisher information matrix. Crucially, its antisymmetric, purely imaginary part encodes geometric information beyond the statistical distance between density operators and plays an essential role in determining the optimal state-conversion rates.

AI.tldr: The maximum linear conversion rates between qubit states of different purities (fixing Bloch vector direction) are governed by the eigenvalues of the complex RLD Fisher information matrix: concentration rates by the maximum-eigenvalue ratio, dilution by the minimum-eigenvalue ratio, and both are achievable using only SWAP tests and maximally mixed ancillas.
AI.motivation: Consuming many copies of an unknown qubit allows modifying purity while preserving the Bloch vector direction, but the fundamental limit on how efficiently such purity conversions can be performed was not established. This work seeks the maximum linear conversion rate under vanishing error and aims to give an operational meaning to the full complex right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information matrix.
AI.method: The authors analyze asymptotic conversion of qubit states of different purities with vanishing trace-distance error in the infinite-copy limit. They derive optimal linear conversion rates in terms of the eigenvalues of the complex RLD Fisher information matrix associated with SU(2) rotations, separately treating concentration and dilution, and show achievability via protocols using SWAP tests as the only nontrivial two-qubit measurement and maximally mixed ancillary qubits, without additional two-qubit gates.
AI.result: For concentration (output purity higher), the optimal rate equals the ratio of the maximum eigenvalues of the input and output RLD matrices; for dilution (output purity lower), it equals the ratio of their minimum eigenvalues. Both tasks are implementable using only SWAP tests plus maximally mixed ancillas. The antisymmetric, purely imaginary part of the complex RLD matrix, encoding geometric information beyond the statistical distance, essentially determines the optimal conversion rates.
AI.conclusion: The full complex RLD Fisher information matrix admits a novel operational interpretation in terms of asymptotic qubit purity conversion, with its eigenvalue structure—including the purely imaginary antisymmetric component—setting the attainable rates. This highlights geometric structure beyond the standard statistical distance and provides resource-frugal protocols based solely on SWAP tests.

title: A complete classification of the existence of finite-dimensional quantum solutions to inconsistent linear constraint systems
summary:
Linear constraint systems (LCS) provide a compact algebraic language for nonlocal games and state-independent contextuality. In the binary case the Mermin--Peres square shows that inconsistent LCS can be solved by promoting variables to local Pauli operators, whereas a series of no-go results excludes analogous Pauli-, Clifford- and monomial unitary-based constructions at odd prime modulus. We first isolate the reason for this difference: for tensor-product quantum solutions, the obstruction to a classical solution of a LCS over $\mathbb{Z}_n$ decomposes into obstruction classes carried by the individual factors. As a consequence, a genuinely global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems. The argument is specific to odd modulus; at even modulus the reordering phase need not vanish, as in Pauli-based examples.
  Given this distinction, we instead associate LCS to finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity in finite-dimensional vector spaces. Quantum solvability for such LCS is automatic and the search for a quantum-classical gap rests entirely on proving classical unsatisfiability of the underlying modular incidence problem of the arrangement. By relating such LCS with group-valued frame functions, we identify a family of examples in the work of [Harding, Jager, and Smith, Int. J. Theor. Phys. 44, 539 (2005)]. To establish the (non)existence of classically unsatisfiable LCS over $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with quantum solutions in all dimensions $d$ and for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we further construct explicit examples for the cases $d=n$ prime. Our main result thus positively resolves the existence problem of such LCS beyond the binary case: such systems exist if and only if $d\geq 3$ and $\gcd(n,d)>1$. Moreover, we establish the existence of LCS with a quantum-classical gap over finite fields if and only if $d\geq 3$ and $p\mid d$.

AI.tldr: The paper explains why global quantum-classical gaps in linear constraint systems (LCS) over odd modulus cannot arise from tensor products of locally unobstructed factors, then constructs LCS from rank-one projector arrangements whose quantum solvability is automatic. It proves such classically unsatisfiable LCS with quantum solutions exist iff d ≥ 3 and gcd(n,d) > 1, and over finite fields iff d ≥ 3 and p | d.
AI.motivation: The Mermin–Peres square shows inconsistent binary LCS can have Pauli-operator quantum solutions, but no-go results exclude analogous Pauli-, Clifford-, and monomial-unitary constructions at odd prime modulus. The paper isolates the structural reason for this difference and seeks to resolve the existence problem for quantum-classical gaps beyond the binary case, for all dimensions d and all n.
AI.method: For tensor-product quantum solutions, the obstruction to a classical solution of an LCS over Z_n is shown to decompose into obstruction classes carried by individual factors, so a genuinely global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems (specific to odd modulus; at even modulus the reordering phase need not vanish). The authors then associate LCS to finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity, making quantum solvability automatic and reducing the gap to classical unsatisfiability of the modular incidence problem. By relating such LCS to group-valued frame functions, they identify examples from Harding–Jager–Smith and construct explicit examples for d = n prime.
AI.result: The obstruction decomposition explains the odd-modulus no-go results versus the even-modulus Pauli-based exceptions. The paper identifies a family of examples in Harding–Jager–Smith (2005) and constructs explicit classically unsatisfiable LCS over Z_n with quantum solutions in all dimensions d and all n ∈ N. The main theorem: such LCS exist iff d ≥ 3 and gcd(n,d) > 1. Over finite fields, LCS with a quantum-classical gap exist iff d ≥ 3 and p | d.
AI.conclusion: The existence problem for classically unsatisfiable LCS with quantum solutions is positively resolved beyond the binary case, with complete characterizations in terms of dimension and modulus (or field characteristic). The obstruction-decomposition argument clarifies the sharp distinction between odd and even modulus, and the projector-arrangement construction provides a systematic framework for generating quantum-classical gaps.

title: Towards Block-Level Fault-Tolerant Quantum Simulation on Small High-Rate Non-CSS Codes
summary: Small high-rate non-CSS stabilizer codes provide compact platforms for encoded quantum computation, but mixed-Pauli checks and limited native transversal logical gates complicate fault-tolerant dynamics. Block-level constructions offer an alternative by mapping an entire logical block to a physical circuit rather than compiling separately protected logical gates. We investigate this approach using the high-rate [[8,3,3]] non-CSS code and logical Trotter circuits as a testbed. We construct flagged syndrome-extraction circuits and establish a circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold near \(1.5\times10^{-3}\). We then apply our symplectic-transvection construction, which maps a logical Trotter circuit to a physical circuit with the same block pattern for any stabilizer code. Although this mapping preserves the intended unitary algebraically, encoded Trotter circuits exhibit asymmetry between logical-\(X\) and logical-\(Z\) failure channels. Single-fault analysis identifies the mechanism: a fault on the shared parity ancilla can propagate through the uncomputation network into an undetectable logical operator, reducing the effective circuit distance in the affected sector. We evaluate flag-conditioned recovery, biased-noise decoding, CliNR resource verification, flag postselection, and asymmetric gate-noise models. These methods suppress propagated faults but do not simultaneously suppress both logical sectors in the realistic configurations studied. A diagnostic protected limit removing the identified malignant first-order locations restores pseudo-threshold behavior in both sectors, approaching memory performance. These results demonstrate the potential of block-level logical constructions for non-CSS codes without rich native transversal gate sets and the joint protection of the parity network, analog rotation, and recovery required to preserve fault-tolerant distance.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates block-level logical constructions for the high-rate [[8,3,3]] non-CSS stabilizer code, building flagged syndrome-extraction circuits with a memory pseudo-threshold near 1.5×10⁻³ and analyzing how encoded Trotter circuits via symplectic transvection exhibit asymmetric logical-X/logical-Z failure channels caused by fault propagation through the parity ancilla network.
AI.motivation: Small high-rate non-CSS stabilizer codes offer compact platforms for encoded quantum computation, but mixed-Pauli checks and limited native transversal logical gates make fault-tolerant dynamics difficult. Block-level constructions—mapping an entire logical block directly to a physical circuit—present an alternative to compiling separately protected logical gates, yet their fault-tolerance properties for non-CSS codes remain underexplored.

They construct flagged syndrome-extraction circuits to establish a circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold, then apply a symplectic-transvection construction that maps a logical Trotter circuit to a physical circuit with the same block pattern for any stabilizer code. They perform single-fault analysis to identify fault-propagation mechanisms and evaluate flag-conditioned recovery, biased-noise decoding, CliNR resource verification, flag postselection, asymmetric gate-noise models, and a diagnostic protected limit.

Encoded Trotter circuits show asymmetry between logical-X and logical-Z failure channels; single-fault analysis reveals that a fault on the shared parity ancilla propagates through the uncomputation network into an undetectable logical operator, reducing effective circuit distance in the affected sector. The mitigation methods studied suppress propagated faults but do not simultaneously suppress both logical sectors in realistic configurations. AI.conclusion: Block-level logical constructions hold potential for non-CSS codes lacking rich native transversal gate sets, but preserving fault-tolerant distance requires joint protection of the parity network, analog rotation, and recovery together.

title: Exact Ionization Amplitudes for a Delta-Function Well in an Arbitrary-Strength DC Electric Field
summary: We investigate finite-time field-induced ionization from a one-dimensional attractive delta-function well in a uniform dc electric field of arbitrary strength. Our aim is to determine the physical bound-state survival amplitude \(a_b(t)\) at any observation time without constructing the complete time-dependent propagator or wavefunction. In the gauge-equivalent Kramers--Henneberger representation, the field appears as motion of the contact point, and the resulting dynamics reduces to a closed Volterra equation. Exact endpoint-phase factorization organizes the full chronological rescattering history into a relative-time convolution hierarchy and an exact resolvent. By introducing the accumulated bound-state amplitude and reorganizing its two-time domain in relative and complementary center times, the final contact contribution becomes an explicit boundary integral. All spatial integrations are carried out analytically. The field-driven contact-free term is obtained in closed form using the Faddeeva function, while the direct and repeated-rescattering terms are expressed as explicitly evaluable time integrals. The result applies at arbitrary dc-field strength and finite time, with no weak-field expansion, rescattering truncation, or asymptotic-time approximation. It is verified through the exact field-free limit and an independent numerical solution of the original physical Volterra equation. The formulation gives an exact nonperturbative solution of a fundamental ionization model and reveals otherwise hidden analytical structure in driven quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact, nonperturbative expression for the bound-state survival amplitude of a 1D attractive delta-function well in an arbitrary uniform dc electric field at finite time, avoiding construction of the full propagator.
AI.motivation: Determining field-induced ionization dynamics (specifically the bound-state survival amplitude) usually requires the full time-dependent propagator or wavefunction, which is difficult. A simpler, exact route is sought for a fundamental ionization model under arbitrary dc-field strength.
AI.method: Works in the gauge-equivalent Kramers-Henneberger representation, where the field appears as motion of the contact point, reducing dynamics to a closed Volterra equation. Exact endpoint-phase factorization reorganized the chronological rescattering history into a relative-time convolution hierarchy plus an exact resolvent. Introducing the accumulated bound-state amplitude and reparametrizing its two-time domain into relative and complementary center times converts the final contact contribution into an explicit boundary integral. All spatial integrations are done analytically; the field-driven contact-free term is expressed via the Faddeeva function, and direct plus repeated-rescattering terms as explicitly evaluable time integrals.
AI.result: An exact closed/near-closed expression for the bound-state survival amplitude at arbitrary dc-field strength and finite time, with no weak-field expansion, rescattering truncation, or asymptotic-time approximation. Verified against the exact field-free limit and an independent numerical solution of the original physical Volterra equation.
AI.conclusion: The formulation provides an exact nonperturbative solution of a fundamental ionization model and exposes hidden analytical structure in driven quantum dynamics.

title: Noise-induced classical phases in optimally-unraveled random quantum circuits
summary: We study the classical simulability of open quantum dynamics using random Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford phase rotations and subject to local noise. We unravel the dynamics into stochastic quantum trajectories simulated with Clifford-augmented matrix product states, and introduce a simulation cost that quantifies the classical resources required. Optimizing this cost over stochastic unravelings, we identify noise-induced classical phases: extended parameter regions in which the dynamics can be fully disentangled by Clifford operations at arbitrary circuit depth. Their existence depends on both the noise model \emph{and} the unraveling. Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, we analytically determine optimal unravelings for a broad class of noise models, with numerical simulations confirming the predicted phase boundaries. We further relate the optimal cost to the unraveling-independent nonstabilizerness of the channel and show that, together with trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness, it classifies distinct dynamical regimes. Finally, we show that these classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where no unraveling freedom remains. Our results show that the emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement scheme adopted to probe it, and paves the way to further studies on the classical simulability of driven-dissipative dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when noisy open quantum dynamics driven by doped Clifford circuits becomes classically simulable, showing that noise can induce "classical phases" disentanglable by Clifford operations — but only under specific unravelings, and these phases vanish in the averaged density-matrix picture.
AI.motivation: Understanding the boundary between classical and quantum behavior in open, noisy quantum dynamics is central to quantum simulation and complexity theory. Prior work on random circuits with non-Clifford gates (e.g., T-gates) established nonstabilizerness-driven complexity, but the role of noise and, crucially, of the stochastic unraveling used to represent it, has remained unclear. The authors aim to determine whether classicality in noisy circuits is intrinsic or dependent on the probing scheme.
AI.method: The authors study random Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford phase rotations under local noise. They unravel the dynamics into stochastic quantum trajectories simulated with Clifford-augmented matrix product states (MPS). They define a simulation cost quantifying the classical resources needed, and optimize it over stochastic unravelings. Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, they analytically derive optimal unravelings for a broad class of noise models, validating predictions numerically. They further connect optimal cost to the unraveling-independent nonstabilizerness of the channel and combine it with trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness to classify dynamical regimes.
AI.result: Noise-induced classical phases emerge: extended parameter regions where dynamics can be fully disentangled by Clifford operations at arbitrary circuit depth. Their existence depends on both the noise model and the unraveling. Optimal unravelings are determined analytically via channel geometry and confirmed by numerics matching predicted phase boundaries. Optimal cost relates to channel nonstabilizerness and, alongside trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness, classifies distinct dynamical regimes. These classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where unraveling freedom is absent.
AI.conclusion: The emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement (unraveling) scheme used to probe it, rather than being a purely intrinsic property. This framework opens the way to further studies on the classical simulability of driven-dissipative quantum dynamics.

title: TSS Graphs for Hadamard Matrices: Real vs Complex
summary:
We have observed that Hadamard matrices whether real or complex lead to a dense output of identical probabilities for any given single input state. Complex Hadamard matrices have unusual orders and introduce phase which prove useful when controlled phase transformation gates are used. By taking a superposed combinations of input states, we discovered that the Hadamards generate non-uniform probabilities which is practically significant towards amplitude amplification without the need for manual parameterization like Grover's operator~\cite{grover1996}. A variety of graph theoretic properties are applied to TSS graphs and their trends were explored. Additionally, graphs turn out to be nearly isomorphic for the same set of input states which has potential applications for developing Quantum Algorithms.
  Keywords: Quantum Algorithms, Hadamard Matrices, Unitary Matrix Approach, Topological Structure of Superpositions (TSS), Graph Theory

AI.tldr: The authors show that Hadamard matrices (real or complex) yield uniform output probabilities for single input states, but produce non-uniform probabilities for superposed input states, enabling amplitude amplification without manual parameterization. Graph-theoretic analysis of TSS graphs reveals near-isomorphism, with potential for quantum algorithm design.
AI.motivation: Grover's operator requires manual parameterization for amplitude amplification. The authors seek a more natural mechanism—using Hadamard matrices—to generate non-uniform probabilities and explore the graph-theoretic structure of superposed states for developing quantum algorithms.
AI.method: The study analyzes real and complex Hadamard matrices, including their unusual orders and phase properties useful in controlled phase transformation gates. It applies a variety of graph-theoretic properties to Topological Structure of Superpositions (TSS) graphs and examines their trends and isomorphism behavior across input states.
AI.result: Single input states yield dense, identical output probabilities for both real and complex Hadamard matrices. Superposed combinations of input states generate non-uniform probabilities. TSS graphs exhibit trends and turn out to be nearly isomorphic for the same set of input states.
AI.conclusion: Hadamard matrices provide a parameterization-free route to non-uniform probability generation and amplitude amplification. The near-isomorphism of TSS graphs offers potential applications for developing quantum algorithms.

title: Why Are We Unrolling? The Importance of Structured Quantum Programs for Compilation
summary: As quantum software stacks scale up to support future fault-tolerant quantum hardware and algorithms, quantum compilation is becoming an increasingly important component of the stack. How do we ensure that our software stacks support dynamic algorithms, including patterns such as mid-circuit measurement feedforward and repeat-until-success, with hundreds of logical qubits and billions of quantum operations? To do so, we must re-think how we represent quantum programs beyond straight-line circuits, to representations that include classical structure and dynamism, and make this the default representation to consider when performing quantum compilation.
