title: QAC0 Can Prepare Every Logarithmic-Qubit State
summary:
$\mathsf{QAC}^0$ is the class of constant-depth $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-ancilla circuits obtained by extending $\mathsf{QNC}^0$, the class of local circuits, to include nonlocal interactions via arbitrary width Toffoli gates. It is believed to be weaker than its counterpart, $\mathsf{QNC}^0_f$, obtained by including arbitrary-width FANOUT gates instead ($\mathsf{QAC}^0 \subseteq \mathsf{QNC}^0_f$ [Moo99]).
  In this note, we show that every $O(\log n)$-qubit state can be exactly and cleanly prepared by a $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-ancilla $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit. Previous known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-ancilla circuits for arbitrary such states are only known via additional access to either FANOUT or QRAM (indexing) gates [Ros21b, GGJ26b], neither of which are known to be in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$. Equivalently, prior constructions of arbitrary $n$-qubit states in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ require doubly exponential size and we obtain an exponential factor improvement.

AI.tldr: Every O(log n)-qubit quantum state can be exactly and cleanly prepared by a poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 circuit, giving an exponential size improvement over prior QAC^0 constructions and removing the need for FANOUT or QRAM gates.
AI.motivation: QAC^0 is believed weaker than QNC^0_f (QAC^0 ⊆ QNC^0_f). Prior poly(n)-ancilla circuits for arbitrary low-qubit states needed FANOUT or QRAM/indexing gates, which are not known to lie in QAC^0; existing QAC^0 constructions of arbitrary n-qubit states required doubly exponential size.
AI.method: Constructively design a poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 circuit, using constant-depth local gates plus arbitrary-width Toffoli gates, that exactly and cleanly prepares any O(log n)-qubit state.
AI.result: Every O(log n)-qubit state admits an exact, clean preparation by a poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 circuit, yielding an exponential factor improvement in circuit size over previous doubly exponential QAC^0 constructions.
AI.conclusion: Arbitrary O(log n)-qubit states are preparable in QAC^0 without FANOUT or QRAM, tightening the relationship between QAC^0 and QNC^0_f and improving state-preparation circuit size exponentially.

title: Sharp bounds for perfect quantum state classification beyond antidistinguishability
summary: A multiset of pure quantum states is said to be k-learnable if there is a measurement strategy that always narrows an unknown sample drawn from the list down to one of at most k candidates. The parameter k interpolates between distinguishability and antidistinguishability, and provides a unified framework for partial state identification. We prove two universal, and optimal, Gram-matrix criteria for k-learnability: a Frobenius-norm sufficient condition and an entrywise-$\ell_1$ necessary condition. We apply them to derive explicit learnability and copy-complexity guarantees for several well-known sets of states including SIC-POVMs, mutually unbiased bases, and stabilizer states. We further apply our results to zero-error mutation detection problems such as anomaly detection and changepoint detection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces k-learnability, a unified framework interpolating between distinguishability (k=1) and antidistinguishability, and proves two universal optimal Gram-matrix criteria (a Frobenius-norm sufficient condition and an entrywise-ℓ1 necessary condition), applying them to SIC-POVMs, MUBs, stabilizer states, and zero-error mutation detection.
AI.motivation: Partial state identification sits between full discrimination and antidistinguishment, but lacked a unified framework and general criteria. The authors aim to fill this gap by defining k-learnability and deriving universal, optimal conditions that yield explicit guarantees for structured state sets and for mutation detection tasks.
AI.method: Define k-learnability via existence of a measurement strategy narrowing an unknown sample to at most k candidates. Prove two universal and optimal Gram-matrix criteria: a Frobenius-norm sufficient condition and an entrywise-ℓ1 necessary condition. Derive explicit learnability and copy-complexity guarantees for SIC-POVMs, mutually unbiased bases, and stabilizer states, and apply the results to zero-error anomaly and changepoint detection.
AI.result: The two Gram-matrix criteria are shown to be universal and optimal. From them, explicit learnability and copy-complexity guarantees are obtained for SIC-POVMs, mutually unbiased bases, and stabilizer states, and the framework yields results for zero-error mutation detection such as anomaly detection and changepoint detection.
AI.conclusion: k-learnability provides a unified, quantitatively sharp framework for partial state identification, with Gram-matrix criteria that are both universal and optimal, and it connects abstract state-identification questions to concrete zero-error detection problems.

title: Evaluating Verified Autonomy in Quantum Engineering
summary: Reliable quantum engineering is essential for turning quantum phenomena into practical technologies. As quantum platforms grow in scale and complexity, their characterization and operation require increasing human effort and coordination. Scientific artificial intelligence agents, which can plan experiments, operate instruments, and analyze observations, offer a promising route towards autonomous quantum engineering. Yet whether current agents can perform reliably in this setting has not been systematically established. To fill this gap, we developed Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory that provides a controlled execution environment for agents to interact with quantum systems. This design enables direct verification of both the actions taken and the conclusions drawn. Building on this framework, we introduce QIQCBench, a benchmark of $49$ expert-authored tasks spanning multiple layers including calibration and control, error correction and compilation, sensing and networking. Across $17$ frontier agentic systems, QIQCBench reveals wide variation in verified performance. These results expose a substantial gap between demonstrating capability and achieving reliable operation, and establish Quantum-Harbor as a foundation for measuring progress towards verified autonomy in quantum engineering.

AI.tldr: Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory with verifiable execution, and QIQCBench, a 49-task benchmark spanning calibration, error correction, compilation, sensing, and networking, reveal large and varied gaps in verified performance across 17 frontier AI agents, exposing the distance between capability and reliable autonomy in quantum engineering.
AI.motivation: Reliable quantum engineering is needed to make quantum technologies practical, but growing platform complexity demands ever more human effort and coordination. AI agents that plan experiments, operate instruments, and analyze observations could enable autonomous quantum engineering, yet it was unknown whether current agents can operate reliably in this setting.
AI.method: The authors built Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory providing a controlled execution environment for agents to interact with quantum systems, which allows direct verification of both actions taken and conclusions drawn. On this basis they created QIQCBench, a benchmark of 49 expert-authored tasks covering multiple layers: calibration and control, error correction and compilation, and sensing and networking. They evaluated 17 frontier agentic systems on it.
AI.result: Across the 17 frontier agentic systems, QIQCBench exposes wide variation in verified performance, revealing a substantial gap between demonstrating capability and achieving reliable operation.
AI.conclusion: Current agents are not yet reliable in autonomous quantum engineering, and Quantum-Harbor establishes a foundation for measuring progress toward verified autonomy in this domain.

title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary:
Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), in which quantum error correction (QEC) suppresses physical errors sufficiently to support reliable logical operations. This requires quantum compilation to move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware and protocol-structured compilation across the full stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond circuit synthesis and hardware mapping, an FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations together with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and provide the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding.
  This survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation. We organize existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. At the logical level, we review surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching. At the physical level, we survey hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. We further examine decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution. Finally, we identify open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at: github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

AI.tldr: A survey of full-stack compiler design for fault-tolerant quantum computation, organized into logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration, with open challenges identified.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), where QEC suppresses physical errors to support reliable logical operations. This demands that quantum compilation move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware, protocol-structured compilation spanning the full stack. Existing treatment is fragmented across circuit synthesis, hardware mapping, logical lowering, ancilla coordination, syndrome extraction, and real-time decoding, so a unified view is needed.
AI.method: The survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation, organizing existing work into three interacting layers: (1) logical-level QEC compilation, reviewing surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching; (2) physical-level QEC realization, surveying hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms; and (3) decoder runtime integration, examining decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution.
AI.result: The survey maps the compiler design space across three interacting layers, showing how algorithm-level operations are lowered into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, how encoded data and ancilla resources are coordinated, how logical operations and repeated syndrome extraction are realized under hardware constraints, and how the resulting measurement stream is provided to real-time decoding.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

title: Predictive Structure Behind Rare Outcomes in Random Quantum Circuits
summary: Rare outputs of random quantum circuits are usually treated as terminal statistics. We ask whether they reveal intermediate organization that remains useful beyond the selecting future. Comparing unconditioned random-normal (RN) and peak-selected random-peaked (RP) circuits from the same local generator, we find stronger pairwise correlations and probability redistribution but reduced bipartite and output spreading in RP across n=8-16. Exact full-suffix decomposition reveals stronger peak-directed interference. The structural separation and fresh-future advantage persist across four nominal depths at n=8-14, with 2.01-7.15 fold RP enrichment in the depth extensions at fixed, independently calibrated thresholds. Within the unconditioned ensemble, a structural prefix score predicts fresh-event probability without using the evaluated circuits' terminal outcomes. Population-preserving phase scrambling identifies a functional contribution from relative-phase organization across the tested settings, including primary-depth held-out confirmation. RP trajectory-guided initialization improves high-peak yield over Haar initialization under common local refinement. Intermediate multivariate guidance also improves the fresh-continuation susceptibility of constructed states beyond peak-only guidance across the same size-depth grid. Rare outputs thus reveal intermediate physical organization that remains useful under new dynamics and can guide circuit construction.

AI.tldr: Rare outputs of random quantum circuits, typically seen as terminal statistics, instead carry intermediate structure that persists under new dynamics and can guide circuit construction.
AI.motivation: The authors question whether rare outputs are merely terminal statistics or whether they reveal intermediate organization useful beyond the selecting future.
AI.method: They compare unconditioned random-normal (RN) and peak-selected random-peaked (RP) circuits from the same local generator, using pairwise correlations, bipartite/output spreading, exact full-suffix decomposition, structural prefix scoring, population-preserving phase scrambling, and trajectory-guided initialization across n=8-16 and multiple depths.
AI.result: RP shows stronger pairwise correlations, probability redistribution, peak-directed interference, but reduced bipartite and output spreading. Structural separation and fresh-future advantage persist across four nominal depths at n=8-14, with 2.01-7.15 fold RP enrichment at fixed calibrated thresholds; prefix scores predict fresh-event probability, phase scrambling shows relative-phase function, and RP/ multivariate guidance improves yields.
AI.conclusion: Rare outputs reveal intermediate physical organization that remains useful under new dynamics and can guide circuit construction.

title: Query-optimal quantum simulation of Lindblad evolution
summary:
For the problem of simulating Lindblad evolution for time $t$ to precision $ε$, Hamiltonian simulation provides an additive query lower bound, informally, $Ω(t + \mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$. However, the best previously known algorithms for general Lindblad simulation achieve a multiplicative upper bound, informally, $\mathcal{O}(t\,\mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$, in gate complexity. It has remained open whether this multiplicative dependence is necessary. In this paper, we close the gap in query complexity by giving an algorithm with optimal additive dependence on evolution time and precision in the block-encoding model. Our approach uses the transducer framework to reduce the query cost of composing first-order approximations to the evolution channel, together with linear combinations of reuse circuits of different lengths to suppress catalyst-removal error.
  Although our additional gate complexity is higher than that of existing algorithms, our optimal query complexity resolves the question of how much oracle access is fundamentally necessary and identifies the remaining challenge to achieve the optimal gate complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper closes the query-complexity gap for general Lindblad evolution simulation by giving an algorithm with optimal additive dependence on evolution time t and precision ε in the block-encoding model, matching the known lower bound Ω(t + polylog(1/ε)), whereas prior algorithms only achieved multiplicative O(t·polylog(1/ε)).
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian simulation provides an additive query lower bound Ω(t + polylog(1/ε)) for Lindblad evolution, but the best previous general Lindblad simulation algorithms only attained a multiplicative upper bound O(t·polylog(1/ε)) in gate complexity. Whether this multiplicative dependence is necessary had remained open.
AI.method: The approach employs a transducer framework to reduce the query cost of composing first-order approximations to the evolution channel, combined with linear combinations of reuse circuits of different lengths to suppress catalyst-removal error.
AI.result: The authors give an algorithm achieving optimal additive dependence on evolution time and precision in query complexity within the block-encoding model, thereby closing the gap with the additive lower bound. Its additional gate complexity is higher than that of existing algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The optimal query complexity resolves the question of how much oracle access is fundamentally necessary for general Lindblad simulation and identifies the remaining challenge of achieving optimal gate complexity.

title: Beyond Hardware: Adaptive Algorithmic Control by State-Proxy Equalization
comment: 15 pages of main text and 30 pages of Supplementary Information
summary: Recent advances in quantum computing have been driven primarily by improvements in hardware. Here we show that substantial gains can instead arise from how finite computational resources are allocated throughout a quantum computation. We introduce Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C), a software paradigm founded on a State-Proxy Equalization theorem, which proves that the optimal allocation for a state-derived proxy-error functional equalizes cumulative computational hardness rather than physical time. The required computational hardness is inferred directly from the evolving quantum state, avoiding explicit reconstruction of the exponentially large many-body spectrum. Across quantum optimization problems containing up to 156 qubits, combining exact simulations, large-scale supercomputer computations and IBM quantum hardware experiments, A2C improves the low-energy sampling probabilities by $22\%$ to over $100,000\%$ under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets. These results demonstrate that quantum computational performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on how finite computational resources are organized, establishing adaptive algorithmic control as a complementary software pathway for advancing quantum computation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C), a software paradigm that improves quantum computation by optimally allocating finite computational resources based on state-derived hardness equalization, boosting low-energy sampling probabilities by 22% to over 100,000%.
AI.motivation: Recent quantum computing advances have focused mainly on hardware improvements. The authors aim to show that substantial gains can instead come from better organizing finite computational resources within a quantum computation, offering a complementary software pathway.
AI.method: The paper proposes A2C, grounded in a State-Proxy Equalization theorem proving that optimal allocation for a state-derived proxy-error functional equalizes cumulative computational hardness rather than physical time. Hardness is inferred directly from the evolving quantum state, avoiding explicit reconstruction of the exponentially large many-body spectrum. Experiments combine exact simulations, large-scale supercomputer computations, and IBM quantum hardware on quantum optimization problems up to 156 qubits.
AI.result: Under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets, A2C improves low-energy sampling probabilities by 22% to over 100,000% across quantum optimization problems up to 156 qubits.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computational performance depends not only on hardware capabilities but also on how finite computational resources are organized, establishing adaptive algorithmic control as a complementary software pathway for advancing quantum computation.

title: Antidistinguishability of states in General Probabilistic Theories
summary: We investigate antidistinguishability of states within the framework of general probabilistic theories (GPTs). We formulate antidistinguishability, strong and equal antidistinguishability as refined notions that imposed additional constraint on the measurement effects. We establish general results relating these notions of antidistinguishability and derive an upper bound on the cardinality of equally antidistinguishable sets in terms of the affine dimension of the state space. We then study antidistinguishability in polygonal theories, obtaining conditions for antidistinguishability of a set of states. In consequence, we show that the set of all pure states in a polygon model is antidistinguishable. Additionally, we identify broad families of strongly and equally antidistinguishable states. Finally, using Random Exclusion Codes, whose success probability is governed by the antidistinguishability of different sets of encoding states, we probe the nonclassicality of polygon theories. We find that certain polygon models can outperform the optimal quantum value, while their optimal performance converges to the quantum limit in the large-polygon limit.

AI.tldr: This paper develops antidistinguishability (including strong and equal variants) in general probabilistic theories, derives dimension-based bounds, characterizes antidistinguishability in polygon models, and uses Random Exclusion Codes to show certain polygon theories exceed optimal quantum performance, converging to the quantum limit as the polygon size grows.
AI.motivation: Antidistinguishability is a fundamental nonclassical feature usually studied in quantum theory; the authors aim to understand how it behaves in the broader framework of general probabilistic theories and to use it as a probe of nonclassicality beyond quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The authors formalize antidistinguishability, strong antidistinguishability, and equal antidistinguishability as notions with extra constraints on measurement effects, establish general relations among them, and derive an upper bound on the cardinality of equally antidistinguishable sets via the affine dimension of the state space. They then analyze polygonal state-space models, deriving conditions for antidistinguishability and identifying families of strongly/equally antidistinguishable states. Finally, they employ Random Exclusion Codes, whose success probability depends on the antidistinguishability of encoding-state sets, to assess nonclassicality.
AI.result: General relations among the three antidistinguishability notions and a dimension-dependent cardinality bound are obtained. In polygon models, conditions for antidistinguishability are derived, and the full set of pure states in a polygon model is shown to be antidistinguishable; broad families of strongly and equally antidistinguishable states are identified. Random Exclusion Codes reveal that some polygon models outperform the optimal quantum value, with performance converging to the quantum limit in the large-polygon limit.
AI.conclusion: Antidistinguishability generalizes meaningfully to GPTs, with polygonal theories providing explicit examples that can surpass quantum performance in Random Exclusion Code tasks while asymptotically approaching the quantum bound, highlighting polygon models as useful testbeds for nonclassicality beyond quantum theory.

title: A Case Study on Noise Resilient Operator Selection in Adaptive Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Hardware noise has been shown to significantly impact the accuracy of ADAPT-VQE, a ground state preparation algorithm. While previous work has studied the impact of noise on its parameter optimization step, its impact on the critical operator selection step remains comparatively unexplored. In this work, we examine the impact of a variety of noise channels on this step, using a linear H$_3$ molecule as a test case. We show that, despite the selection criterion's natural resilience to some noise, both coherent and incoherent noise can prevent convergence for sufficiently high noise rates. We employ quantum error mitigation techniques--dynamical decoupling, zero noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling--and show that when combined appropriately, these techniques are capable of restoring a successful convergence profile. Our results highlight how error mitigation can improve the performance of ADAPT-VQE and enable convergence in the presence of hardware noise, offering valuable insights into the implementation of the algorithm on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This work studies how hardware noise affects the operator selection step of ADAPT-VQE for a linear H3 molecule, and shows that combining dynamical decoupling, zero noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling restores convergence under noise.
AI.motivation: Hardware noise degrades ADAPT-VQE accuracy. Prior studies focused on the parameter optimization step, while the impact of noise on the critical operator selection step was largely unexplored.
AI.method: Using a linear H3 molecule as a test case, the authors examine the effect of various noise channels (coherent and incoherent) on the operator selection criterion. They then apply quantum error mitigation techniques—dynamical decoupling, zero noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling—individually and in combination.
AI.result: The selection criterion is naturally resilient to some noise, but both coherent and incoherent noise can prevent convergence at sufficiently high noise rates. When combined appropriately, the error mitigation techniques restore a successful convergence profile.
AI.conclusion: Error mitigation can improve ADAPT-VQE performance and enable convergence under hardware noise, providing insights for implementing the algorithm on near-term quantum hardware.
